text: Welcome to the Beginner Capstone for the Analytics Engineer path. Over these ten lessons you're going to take one real stakeholder complaint, all the way from a frustrated hallway comment to a tested dbt model running on Snowflake. Lesson one starts where every real analytics-engineering project actually starts: before any dbt, before any SQL, with a conversation.

Here's the ask. You're the analytics engineer at Jaffle Shop — the same real sample e-commerce business the dbt course earlier in this catalog already uses. The Ops Manager stops by, clearly annoyed, and says: our customer data is a mess, finance has one spreadsheet, support has another, nobody agrees on how many customers we actually have, I just want ONE list I can trust. Sounds simple. It isn't, yet — because that sentence is hiding real questions. Our customer data — where does it actually live? One list — of what, exactly? I can trust — trust means what, specifically? And is this just about customers, or does it quietly also want orders and payments bundled in?

The fix isn't guessing. It's a short follow-up conversation that nails down four things: the source, the scope, the grain, and a concrete definition of trust. Five minutes here saves you from building the wrong thing and finding out only after you've already written the models.

Once you ask, the vague complaint turns into something specific. It turns out Jaffle Shop already has raw data sitting in Snowflake — raw_customers, raw_orders, raw_payments — loaded by an earlier process. This project's real ask becomes: build a single, tested customer table, sourced from the existing raw_customers data, one row per customer, with a guaranteed non-null, unique customer ID — something finance and support can both query and get the same answer from. That sentence is the real spec for this entire project.

Just as important as what's in scope is what's deliberately left out. In scope: one staging model, one mart model, real dbt tests proving the data is trustworthy. Out of scope: joining in orders and payments — that's the next project in this series, the Intermediate capstone. Also out of scope: CI/CD, production scheduling, anything beyond this one clean deliverable. Matching your effort to the actual ask is part of doing this well.

That's the business ask, turned into a real requirement. Next lesson, we start translating that requirement into a plan for the dbt project itself — the three layers you'll build, named explicitly, before a single file gets created.
